subsection: 5. Legal control of additives in the EU

notes.b: The use of food additives in the European Union is controlled by Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, which sets rules for preservatives, colourings, emulsifiers and antioxidants, among other additives.
points: As an EU regulation, it applies directly in Ireland without needing a separate Irish Act.
An additive may be used only if it appears on the approved list of additives for the EU.
Each additive must be tested for safety before it is approved.
Each approved additive is assigned an E number, except flavourings, which are not given E numbers.

notes.h: E numbers and the classes they identify
points: E100 to E199 are colourings, for example E150 caramel and E102 tartrazine.
E200 to E299 are preservatives, for example E202 potassium sorbate and E220 sulphur dioxide.
E300 to E399 are antioxidants, for example E300 vitamin C and E320 BHA; the range also includes acidity regulators.
E400 to E499 are thickeners, stabilisers and emulsifiers, for example E322 lecithin.
E600 to E699 are flavour enhancers, for example E621 monosodium glutamate.
E900 to E999 include sweeteners, for example E950 acesulfame K, E951 aspartame, E954 saccharin and E955 sucralose.
An additive must not reduce the nutritive value of the food.
An additive must not be used to disguise poor quality or faulty processing.
An additive must not present a health hazard to the consumer.
An additive must not mislead the consumer about the food.
Each additive must be used in the smallest quantity needed to achieve its effect.
Colourings are not permitted in fresh fruit, fresh vegetables, fresh meat, poultry or fish.
Colourings are not permitted in baby food, and sweeteners are not permitted in food for infants and young children.
The label must show the class name of the additive followed by its specific name or E number, for example preservative: sulphur dioxide or preservative: E220.
Flavourings are declared by name rather than by an E number.
Consumers can therefore identify the function and the approved status of an additive from its label.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland is responsible for enforcing the safe use of food additives in Ireland.

Official agencies working under FSAI service contracts, including the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the HSE Public Analyst Laboratories and local authorities, check compliance through inspection and sampling.
The FSAI advises ministers, regulators, industry and consumers, and processes applications for new foods and processing methods.

keyTerms.definition: The EU regulation on food additives, which sets the approved list, conditions of use and labelling rules for additives in the European Union.
The EU list of additives that have been tested for safety and are permitted for use in specified foods.
A code beginning with E, given to each approved additive, which identifies it on the label.
The least amount of an additive needed to achieve its intended effect in a food.
The amount of nutrients a food supplies, which an additive must not reduce.
Food made for infants and young children, to which EU rules restrict or forbid certain additives.
The checking, sampling and inspection carried out by official bodies to ensure that food law is obeyed.
The Irish body that coordinates national food safety enforcement, including the safe use of food additives.

questions.prompt: Explain why a food label must show the E number or name of each additive, and state the legal basis for the control of additives in the EU.
questions.model: The label lets the consumer identify each additive and its function, so the consumer can check whether it is approved and make an informed choice; it also supports enforcement, since officials can check that approved additives are used correctly. Legal basis: Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, which applies directly in Ireland, requires an approved list, E numbers for approved additives (except flavourings) and labelling of the additive's class name and specific name or E number.

questions.prompt: Outline how European Union law controls the use of food additives in Ireland, covering approval, conditions of use and labelling, and name the Irish body that enforces the rules.
questions.model: Approval: an additive may be used only if it is on the EU approved list, which means it has been tested for safety and is assigned an E number (flavourings excepted). Conditions of use: an additive must not reduce nutritive value, disguise faulty processing, present a health hazard or mislead the consumer, and must be used in the smallest effective quantity; colourings are not permitted in fresh fruit, vegetables, meat, poultry or fish, and colourings and sweeteners are restricted in baby food and food for young children. Labelling: the class name and the specific name or E number of each additive must be on the label, so the consumer can identify it. Enforcement: the Food Safety Authority of Ireland enforces the safe use of additives, with official agencies such as the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, the HSE Public Analyst Laboratories and local authorities checking compliance by inspection and sampling.
